---
title: "Palettes and colour"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8.8, fig.height = 4.4, dpi = 100,
  fig.retina = 2, dev = "ragg_png", out.width = "100%"
)
options(gglaplot2.font = "inter")
library(ggplot2)
library(gglaplot2)
```

Colour on a chart does one of four jobs: it tells series apart, it shows how
much, it shows which side of a midpoint, or it names a state. The palettes
are built from the `data-*` and `palette-*` tokens for those jobs.

```{r swatches, fig.height = 3.6}
gla_show_pal()
```

## Categorical

The categorical palette is the order the web charts colour series in:
`data-primary`, `data-secondary`, `data-tertiary`, then turquoise, purple,
red, green and yellow. A chart here and a chart on one of the visualisation
team's sites colour the fourth series alike. It validates clean to three
series under the palette checks (lightness, chroma, colour vision deficiency
separation, contrast on the surface); past three, turquoise reads grey on a
light surface and red against green is a known pair. Design to three and fold
categories rather than reach for a fourth colour; where a chart must carry
more, label the series directly. Asking for more colours than the palette has
is an error, not a recycled colour.

```{r}
gla_pal("categorical")
gla_max_series()
```

## Series rules

`scale_colour_gla()` and `scale_fill_gla()` default to `type = "auto"`, which
reads the level names the way the web charts do. London against one
comparator is `data-primary` against `data-context`: London is the subject and
the comparator a reference.

```{r london}
d <- data.frame(
  year = rep(2015:2024, 2), area = rep(c("London", "England"), each = 10),
  value = c(cumsum(rnorm(10, 1)) + 20, cumsum(rnorm(10, 0.5)) + 20)
)
ggplot(d, aes(year, value, colour = area)) +
  geom_gla_line() +
  geom_gla_endlabel(aes(label = area)) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.15))) +
  scale_colour_gla() +
  gla_labs(title = "London against England", subtitle = "An index", x = NULL) +
  theme_gla(legend = "none")
```

Domestic against International, and Inner against Outer London, are primary
against secondary. Anything else is the palette in order, with London moved
to the front. The rule on its own is `gla_series_colours()`.

```{r}
gla_series_colours(c("Inner London", "Outer London"))
gla_series_colours(c("England", "Wales", "London"))
```

## Sequential and diverging

The sequential palette is the blue ramp, light to dark, interpolated to any
number of steps. The diverging palette runs red through a neutral grey to
blue, the same colours the change palette uses for down and up.

```{r}
gla_pal("sequential", 7)
gla_pal("diverging", 5)
```

```{r ramps, fig.height = 5}
ggplot(gla_boroughs) +
  geom_gla_sf(aes(fill = nchar(name))) +
  scale_fill_gla_c(name = NULL) +
  gla_labs(title = "A sequential ramp", subtitle = "Letters in the borough name") +
  theme_gla_map()
```

## Sex and change

`"sex"` maps women and men by level name, under both spellings a source
might use, so the colours never swap when the levels reorder. `"change"`
maps `up` and `down`: a value rising is coloured by the token, not by its
arithmetic sign.

```{r}
gla_pal("sex")
gla_pal("change")
```

## Checking a palette

The checks the palettes are held to can be run on any set of colours.
`gla_check_palette()` is the categorical set: the lightness band, the chroma
floor, separation between neighbours under simulated colour vision
deficiency and under normal vision, and contrast on the surface.
`gla_check_ramp()` is the set for an ordered ramp. The package's tests run
both on every palette, so a token release that moves a colour out of bounds
fails the suite rather than reaching a chart.

```{r}
gla_check_palette(gla_pal(n = 3))
gla_check_palette(gla_pal())
gla_check_ramp(gla_pal("sequential", 5))
```

## Dark mode

Every palette has a dark reading. Pass `theme = "dark"` to the scale when
the chart uses `theme_gla(theme = "dark")`.

```{r dark-swatches, fig.height = 3.6}
gla_show_pal(theme = "dark")
```
